title: The Horse That "Did Math"… and Fooled Berlin 🐴🧮

yt_description:
In the early 1900s, Wilhelm von Osten showed Berlin a horse named Hans that seemed to count, add and tell time by tapping its hoof. In 1904 a commission of experts found no tricks. Then psychologist Oskar Pfungst tested him: Hans was right 89% of the time when he could see the questioner, and only 6% when he couldn't; if the questioner didn't know the answer, Hans failed too. Hans was reading tiny, unconscious cues: tension as the taps neared the answer, then a slight lift of the head at the right tap.
Today scientists call it the Clever Hans effect.

script: In the early 1900s, Berlin fell in love with a horse named Hans. His owner, a math teacher called Wilhelm von Osten, said Hans could count, add, and even tell time. Ask Hans what two plus three is, and he tapped his hoof five times. Then stopped. Crowds came. Von Osten never charged admission. People called him Clever Hans. In 1904, a commission of experts studied the horse. Their verdict: no tricks. Then psychologist Oskar Pfungst tried something simple. He changed who asked the questions, and what they could see. When Hans could see the questioner, he was right eighty-nine percent of the time. When he couldn't, only six percent. And if the questioner didn't know the answer, neither did Hans. Hans wasn't doing math. He was reading people. As the taps got close to the right number, the questioner tensed up. At the right tap, they relaxed, with a tiny lift of the head. That was his signal to stop. Nobody was cheating. The humans didn't even know they were doing it. This is called the Clever Hans trap. Scientists call it the Clever Hans effect. When you expect an answer, you can leak it without knowing. Into tests, into interviews, even into the AI you train. So before you trust a result, ask: did it find the answer, or did it find me?
